text:
Jordan made a circle in the dirt with his finger. It was his own little spot in the school garden. Miss Ana gave him three seeds to plant. Jordan pushed the seeds down, not too deep. Then he covered them up with soft brown dirt. He gave the seeds a drink of water from his small green can.

The next morning, Jordan ran to the garden. He looked and looked. There was only dirt in his circle. No sprout was up yet. "Maybe they need more water," said Miss Ana. So Jordan watered the seeds again. Every day he came back. Every day he shared his water with the dirt.

Then one morning, something small and green stood up in the dirt. It was a sprout! Jordan clapped his hands. "Hello, little sprout," he said. "I will bring you more water tomorrow."

Romy wanted her teddy bear. He sat high on the toy shelf. Romy was small. The shelf was big.

She pushed her toy truck to the shelf. The truck went fast. Then it went slow, slow, slow. It stopped. Romy was mad at the truck. "You did not help," she said.

Then she saw the stepping stool. Papa had put it by the shelf. It had a yellow sign on it that said Romy. She climbed up, up, up. She reached the teddy bear! Then she climbed down, down, down.

Papa came in with warm cocoa. "Careful, it is hot," he said. He held the cup while Romy hugged the cold teddy bear tight.

"Papa, up and down are opposites," said Romy. "I went up to get him. I came down to hug him."

Papa smiled. "You teach me something new every day."

Then teddy's hat fell off. A tiny mouse toy was hiding under it! "A surprise!" said Romy. She put the mouse in teddy's lap and gave them both a kiss.

Willow loved playtime at school. Today the teacher put out three big mats. "Let us sort," said Miss Kim. "Animals go here. Toys go there. Foods go on the blue mat."

Willow picked up a little cow. She put it on the animal mat. She picked up a soft ball. She put it with the toys. Then she saw something funny. A banana was hiding among the toy cars!

"Look," said Willow. "The banana does not fit here." Her friend Sam ran over. "It is the odd one out," said Sam. "It is the one that does not belong in the group." Willow held the banana up. The cars were all the same hard toys. The banana was soft food.

Willow put the banana on the blue food mat. Miss Kim smiled. "You learn fast," she said. Willow clapped her hands. "A mat is a good tool for sorting!" she said. Then she ran back to find more odd ones out.

Felix stood in the band room. He held a little drum. He wanted to play a song all by himself.

Miss Jo showed him a big paper. It had dots and lines on it. "What are those?" Felix asked. "Those are notes," said Miss Jo. "Written music uses notes to show which sounds to play." Felix tapped the drum. Miss Jo pointed to a note. He tapped again. She pointed to the next note. He tapped that one too.

Felix felt upset when he missed a note. "Slow down," said Miss Jo. "Try again." So he tried again. And again. A bird sat by the window and seemed to listen. Felix looked at the notes, one by one. He tapped each one. Tap, tap, tap. Then he played them all in a row.

"Look at me!" said Felix. Miss Jo clapped. Felix climbed off his little stool and took a bow. The bird flew up, and Felix tapped one more note.

Edouard ran into the playroom. He wanted to sing his monkey song! He put five toy monkeys on the bed. "One, two, three, four, five!" he counted. He loved to count. Sometimes he counted all the way to ten, fast, just for fun.

Edouard sang, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed!" Then one monkey fell off and bumped his head. Edouard put that monkey on the rug. Now he counted again. "One, two, three, four!" There were four monkeys on the bed!

He sang the next verse. Another monkey fell off! "One, two, three!" This was big news. Each time he sang, one monkey fell off, and the number got one smaller. It was his turn to sing again, so he sang loud.

Soon one little monkey sat alone on the bed. All the rest were on the rug, next to a smudge of dirt Edouard wiped with his sock. Edouard picked up the last monkey. "No more monkeys!" he sang. Then he hugged all ten toy animals together.

Evelyn lived in a little house with her mama. One morning, Mama put on a song. The song had a steady beat. Evelyn patted her knees, but too fast. Mama clapped slow. Clap, clap, clap. Evelyn tried again, slow like Mama. Clap, clap, clap. Now her claps fit the song.

Then Mama sang a rhyme. "The cat sat on the red hat." Evelyn wanted to sing it too. She sang, "The cat sat on the..." Then she stopped. The next word was gone. She could not find it.

She looked at the floor. There was her red block. She held the block and thought. Hat. Block did not sound right at the end. She tried more words in her head. Cat, hat, bat, mat. "Mat!" said Evelyn. "The cat sat on the mat!" Mama laughed and clapped. "Yes! Mat rhymes with cat. Both end the same."

Evelyn stood up tall. She sang the whole rhyme. She clapped on the beat while she sang. Clap, clap, clap. Mama clapped too. Evelyn sang it one more time, all by herself.

"Again, Mama!" said Evelyn. "Sing it again!"

Clara loved school. At school she counted things. One, two, three cups. One, two, three chairs. The big kids ran fast in the yard. Clara walked slow and looked at the floor.

At lunch, her soup was hot. The teacher carried the pot. Clara held her cold milk. "Careful," said Miss Posy. "Big pot, hot soup. Little cup, cold milk." Clara blew on her spoon. Then she put it down. It was nap time.

Clara slept a long time. She woke up and saw dark. She sat up fast. "Is it morning?" she asked. Miss Posy smiled. "Look out the window," she said. Clara looked. The sky was black. A wild owl flapped one wing, then two. "It is still night," said Miss Posy. "Day and night are opposites." Clara lay back down. She counted soft stars. One, two, three. She closed her eyes.

Later the sky turned light. The day was back. Clara ran to the window. "Good morning, sun," she said. One, two, three birds flew by.

Parker stood by the green pool wall. The water went splash, splash. His feet did not want to go in. "Too big," said Parker. Up on the tall chair sat a lady in a red suit. "Who is that?" Parker asked. "That is the lifeguard," said Dad. "Her job is to watch the swimmers and help anyone who needs it." Parker looked up. She could see every kid from up there. She waved at him. Parker sat down at the edge. He put one toe in. The water was warm. He kicked his legs. The water made little waves. His toy boat began to float away. Parker chased it with his toes. The lifeguard saw him lean too far. She climbed down fast. "Hold my hand," she said. Parker held it and stepped in. "Yay!" said Parker. "I am swimming with help." Dad clapped. The boat bumped against Parker's tummy. The lifeguard smiled and went back up high to watch.

Rehmat wanted to play the shouting game with her big brother. He said a word, and she had to shout back the opposite. "Opposites are two words as different as they can be," he said. Then he began.

"Big!" he shouted. Rehmat looked around the playroom. She pointed at the big teddy bear. Then she held up a small sock. "Small!" she shouted. Her brother laughed and clapped.

"Fast!" he said. Rehmat ran fast across the room. Then she walked slow, slow, slow, like a sleepy turtle. The game got tricky. "Hot!" he said. Rehmat pointed at the kitchen. "Daddy's tea is hot," she said. Her daddy waved and held the cup far away, so she would not touch. "Cold!" she shouted next, and hugged the cold window glass.

Rehmat got one wrong. Her brother said "Up," and she shouted "Cat." She felt grumpy and sat on the floor. "Big and small are different," her brother said. "Up and down are different too. You almost had it." Rehmat stood up. "Down!" she shouted. He gave her a gold star letter, her very own S. She held it tight and smiled. "Again!" she said.

Audrey sat in the school library. She wanted to write her name. But the K kept coming out wrong. It looked funny every time. Audrey frowned at her paper.

The librarian gave her a bumpy card. The letter K was raised up on it. Audrey put her finger on the card. She traced the shape, top to bottom, then out and out again. The bumps tickled her finger. She traced it one more time.

Then she picked up her pencil. Her arm moved slow and careful. She wrote the K. This time it was right! Audrey made the K sound, "k, k, k." She wrote A, U, D, R, E, Y too. Her whole name sat on the paper, just right. Audrey held it up high. "Look what I can do!"

Today was Diwali. Madeline looked at her toy box. She held up her old play shorts. She held up her blue sweater with a hole near the tooth pocket. None of them felt right. Grandma came in with a red dress. It had tiny gold stars. "People often wear special clothes to a celebration," Grandma said. Madeline touched the soft red fabric. She put it on. The dress went swish when she turned. Downstairs, Daddy was lighting little lamps. He used the matches himself, and Madeline watched from her chair. The lamps made warm circles on the table. Outside the window the sky looked dark and stormy. Inside, the lamps glowed and the sweets sat on a big plate. Madeline spun once more in her red dress. "Happy Diwali," she said.

Max sat at Grandma's kitchen table. He had a big pencil and a paper. Max wanted to write his name all by himself. His brother could write his name, but Max was still young. Max tried to make an M. It came out wobbly and crooked. He tried again. It looked like a squiggle worm. Max frowned at the paper.

Grandma slid a new paper to him. It had the letters M A X on it. Each letter was made of little dots. "Trace the dots," said Grandma. Max put his pencil on the first dot. He drew a line to the next dot. Then the next one. The dots made an M. A real M. Max made a happy sound.

He traced the A and the X too. Then he found a dry spot on the paper. He wrote M A X with no dots. He looked at it. Was that his name? He held the paper up high. "Look, Grandma! I wrote Max!"

"You did," said Grandma. She clapped her hands. Max turned the paper over. There was a blank side. Maybe he could write it again. He picked up his pencil and began.

Snow fell all night long. Abigail looked out the window. Her eyes went wide. "Snow!" she said. Mama said, "Put on your boots. Put on your warm coat." Abigail zipped her coat up high.

They walked to the park. Snow covered the slide and the swings. Abigail forgot her hat and mittens. She made a snowball with bare hands. Soon her fingers hurt. They were red and cold. "My hands are too cold," she said. Mama had the hat and mittens in her pocket. "Try again," said Mama. Abigail put them on. Her fingers got warm again. She clapped her mittens together. Clap, clap!

Then Abigail saw something in the snow. A small green frog sat by the pond. It hopped away, hop, hop, hop. Abigail laughed and waved. "Bye, frog!" she called. Then she built a big snowman, warm from her hat to her boots.

Ivy sat on the grass by Grandpa's stone. It was gray and smooth. Mama set out a picnic on a dry cloth. There were bread, cheese, and red apples.

"Hold hands," said Mama. "We say our blessing first." Ivy did not know the blessing yet. She held Mama's hand and Daddy's hand. The bread smelled warm. Her tummy growled. But she waited.

"Thank you for our food," Mama said slowly. "Thank you for this day." Then Daddy said it too. Ivy looked at the apple in her hand. Somebody grew this apple. Somebody picked it. She wanted to say that.

"Now me," said Ivy. She took a big breath. "One, thank you for the bread. Two, thank you for the cheese. Three, thank you for the apples. Four, thank you for the people who grew them." She squeezed Mama's hand. Mama smiled. Daddy clapped softly.

After the blessing, they ate. Ivy bit her apple. It was sweet and cold. She put a small piece of bread by the stone, just for Grandpa. "He can share too," she said. A bird flew down and hopped near the cloth. "Look, Mama," said Ivy. "Even the bird says thank you."

Evelyn woke up in her bed. She heard a spoon in a bowl. She ran to the table. Mama and Papa were there, eating eggs.

"Good morning, Evelyn," said Mama.

Evelyn climbed into her chair. "Good morning," she said back. She ate her eggs too. Morning was the time when they woke up and ate breakfast. Then it was time for the park.

At the park, the sun was wide and bright. Evelyn ran to the swing. But a boy was on it.

"Can I have a turn later?" Evelyn asked.

"Yes," said the boy. "Later, when I count to ten."

Evelyn waited. The boy counted slowly. One, two, three. He counted all the way to ten. Then he jumped off.

"Now it is my turn," said Evelyn.

Mama pushed her high. Evelyn held on tight.

"Yesterday I could not swing," said Evelyn. "Yesterday the swing was wet."

"Today it is dry," said Mama. "Today you can swing."

"And tomorrow?" asked Evelyn.

"Tomorrow we can come back," said Mama.

After the swing, they sat on the grass. Evelyn found a dandelion. It was gone to seed, all white and round.

"Make a wish," said Mama. "Then blow."

Evelyn took a big breath. She blew. The little seeds flew up and away. They floated over the sandbox. They floated past the big tree.

Evelyn looked at the empty stem. "My wish is gone," she said.

"It is not gone," said Mama. "It went with the seeds."

Evelyn smiled. She put the stem in Mama's hand.

"Put it in my pocket," said Mama. "It can be my present."

They walked home slowly. The sun was going down.

"Good night, park," said Evelyn. She waved her hand.

Lillian ran to the toy box. She wanted to build a house for her toy snake. She found a block with four flat sides. "A square!" she said.

Lillian stacked the square on top. Then it slipped. It turned on its side. Now one corner pointed up. Her brother Ben peeked in. "That is a new shape," he said. "No it isn't," said Lillian. She grabbed the block. She gave it a turn. The corner went down. The flat side sat on the floor. "Look! It is the same square," she said. Ben clapped. "The square was hiding!"

Lillian used the square for the door. She found two triangles for the roof. A circle became a window. A long rectangle made a bed. The silly snake slid right in. "Home at last," said Ben. Lillian smiled and rang a little bell.

Charles went to the art studio with his papa. He brought his box of crayons. Yesterday he had left the box in the family car. The car sat in the sun all day.

Charles opened the box. "Oh no," he said. The crayons were soft. They were bendy too. One crayon bent like a little snake. "They were hard before," said Charles. Papa nodded. "The car was hot," he said. "Crayons can melt in a hot car on a sunny day."

Charles wanted to draw a sun. But the crayons were too soft. He pressed one on the paper. It made a shiny smudge. He pressed again. The smudge got bigger. Charles tried a red crayon. He made a shiny red sun, all smudgy and bright.

Then he mixed the red smudge with a yellow smudge. He rubbed with his finger. The red and yellow made orange. The orange sun looked warm and round.

Charles made smudge clouds too. He made a smudge green hill. He used his soft bendy crayons the whole time. "I like soft crayons," said Charles. Papa smiled. "Let's keep them out of the hot car," he said. Charles held up his picture. "My sun is shiny," he said.

Ibrahim was at the park with his dad. He brought his little blue car. It was his favorite toy. He set it on the picnic table. Then he ran to the slide. When he came back, the car was gone.

"Where is my car?" said Ibrahim. He looked by the swing. No car. He looked in the grass. No car. He looked near the water fountain. No car. He tried one more look at the table. Still no car.

Dad sat down on the long bench. He patted the seat. "Small toys can roll or slide under furniture," said Dad. Ibrahim got down on his knees. He peeked under the bench. It was dark and cool there. He saw dust and a candy wrapper. Then he saw something blue. It was his car! It had rolled right under the bench.

Ibrahim reached in and pulled it out. The car felt cold from the shade. He held it up to the sun. "Found you!" he said. Then he put the car deep in his pocket, where it could not roll away, and ran back to the slide with Dad.

Lily woke up on her mat. The room was dark and quiet. "Is it night?" she whispered. She wanted her mommy.

Miss Kay came over. She opened the curtain. The sun came in. It was bright. "It is day," said Miss Kay. "Day and night are opposites." Lily looked out. One sun, one big blue sky. Not night at all. She felt better.

It was time to go outside. Lily put on her shoes. She found her cubby. It had a letter L on it. "L is for Lily," she said. Outside, the sun felt hot on her hands. Then she sat in the shade. The shade felt cold. "Hot sun, cold shade," she said.

Lily wanted the big swing. But Ben was on it. He went fast, fast, fast. Lily waited on the small swing. She went slow, slow, slow. Then she saw a snail on the wall. Its trail was slimy. "Yuck," she said, and she wiped her hand on her dress. Ben jumped off the big swing. "Your turn, Lily!" he did shout. Lily ran. One, two, three, she climbed up. "Push me slow," she said. "Then push me fast."
